newsitem.title: INDIA: India's wheat imports have little impact on market.
newsitem.headline: India's wheat imports have little impact on market.

text.p: India's recent decision to import two million tonnes of wheat to augment supplies and check prices has had a limited impact due to faulty planning, analysts and trade officials said on Thursday.
"The intervention from the government came late," Tarun Kumar, an official at Delhi foodgrains exporter Space Group told Reuters.
"Prices have not stabilised considerably. By the time all the imports come in, the new crop will also be in," he said.
In December, India authorised the state-run State Trading Corporation (STC) to import two million tonnes of wheat in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) to build stocks and check rising prices.
Traders said wheat prices in domestic markets were now trading at an average of 7,150 rupees ($200) per tonne, compared with a high of 7,700 rupees in October and November.
STC officials said it had so far contracted for imports of 1.7 million tonnes of wheat, mainly from Australia, Canada and Argentina.
"So far about 800,000 tonnes of imported wheat shipments have arrived," said one STC official. He added the 1.7 million tonnes would arrive in Indian ports by the end of April.
But analysts said the shipments were likely to be delayed beyond April due to handling and berthing problems at Indian ports.
"The imports have helped marginally. They are trying to replenish government stocks," said Ashok Gulati of the independent National Council of Applied Economic Research.
Kumar said the government should have taken the decision to import in September or October so that all the imports would have arrived by December.
He said a timely decision to import the entire quantity in one lot would have brought out all the hoarded stocks, and stabilised prices.
Hoarded stocks were just trickling out and not having the desired impact on prices, he added.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament this week that India's wheat stocks on April 1 were projected at 2.72 million tonnes, down one million tonnes from the buffer stock norms of 3.7 million tonnes set by the government.
Officials of the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI), the country's largest grain trading agency, said it had begun wheat procurement from March 17, against the normal start date of April 1.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 marketing season fell to 8.2 million tonnes from 12.3 million tonnes in the previous year due to a three million tonne shortfall in output.
India expects a wheat crop of about 64.5 million tonnes in 1996/97 (July/June), up sharply from 62.6 million produced in 1995/96.
Officials said rust disease in the northern state of Punjab and high temperatures during harvesting time in March 1996 had contributed to low output in 1995/96.
Gulati said it was the right time for the government to open up the wheat trade to both import and exports.
